description: We are building EmberAtlas, a satellite-based platform that integrates MODIS and VIIRS active fire detection data to visualize hotspots, explore historical patterns, and identify unusual fire activity. We are interested in software development, data science, geospatial analysis, and Earth observation. We welcome motivated participants who want to collaborate, learn, and build a meaningful project using NASA data.
summary: EmberAtlas is a web application that harmonizes NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS (Terra/Aqua, 2000–present) and VIIRS S-NPP (2012–present) into one consistent burning-activity calendar for Colombia. Raw VIIRS sees about three times more burning cell-days than MODIS, which creates an artificial jump in 2012. We aggregate detections to a common ~1 km grid, convert VIIRS to MODIS-equivalent values with block-by-month factors calibrated on 2013–2019, and evaluate them on 2020–2026 (median error ≈12% per 1° block-year; ≈80% of national months within ±20% of MODIS). Users draw an area of interest, choose a date range, and get a year × month heatmap with an accessible color ramp, the latest month compared with the historical median and percentiles for the same calendar month, and a CSV of the original detections. Limitations are stated openly: the first 20 months rely on Terra only, and MODIS orbits drift after 2020. Developed with AI assistance (see SI disclosure).
details:
EmberAtlas is an interactive web platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge that merges more than two decades of NASA FIRMS active-fire observations — MODIS C6.1 (Terra/Aqua, 2000–present) and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m (2012–present) — into a single, consistent time series for Colombia.

How it works

- Users draw an area of interest on the map or enter exact coordinates, and select a date range.

- A year × month burning-activity calendar with accessible color ramps (Viridis for activity, ColorBrewer PuOr for anomalies).

- The latest complete month compared with the historical median of the same calendar month (2003–2025), with the p10–p90 normal range and the percentile.

- A raw vs. harmonized time-series chart that shows how the sensor-transition jump is corrected.

- A CSV export of the original FIRMS detections for the selected area and dates (up to 200,000 rows).

Benefits and impact

Simply stitching the MODIS (~1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) records creates an artificial jump in 2012: in Colombia, raw VIIRS sees about 3.2 times more burning cell-days than MODIS. EmberAtlas puts both records on one scale, so emergency managers, firefighters, environmental agencies and scientists can compare any month with its own history and spot months that are unusual for an area, without worrying about which sensor observed them. The method, validation and limitations are documented openly in the repository.

Tools and tech stack

- Data engineering and backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, DuckDB, Apache Parquet (PyArrow), pandas and NumPy, running locally over 2.31 million FIRMS detections.

- Frontend and visualization: React, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet (React Leaflet) and Recharts.

- Hardware: standard desktop PC running Windows 11.

Creativity and considerations

EmberAtlas is a lightweight web application that tackles a known inconsistency between the MODIS and VIIRS fire records. Key technical choices:

- Scientific rigor: detections are binned onto a common 0.01° (~1.1 km) grid and counted as burning cell-days instead of raw hotspots, which reduces the VIIRS overcount.

- Spatiotemporal calibration: VIIRS/MODIS conversion factors per 1° × 1° block and calendar month, fitted on 2013–2019 (stable Terra and Aqua orbits) and shrunk toward the national factor (prior weight K = 100). MODIS is used as observed until 2019; from 2020, VIIRS is divided by its factor to give MODIS-equivalent values.

- Validation: evaluated on 2020–2026 against MODIS, the median error is 11.7% per 1° block-year, and 66 of 82 national months (80%) fall within ±20% of MODIS. K was tuned on the same period, so these errors are somewhat optimistic.

- Transparency: Terra-only months (Nov 2000–Jun 2002) are hatched and excluded from anomalies, and the interface warns when the two sensors differ by more than 20% in the latest month.

Limitations

Colombia only (a bounding box, not the national border: neighboring areas show no data, not zero fires); MODIS orbits drift after 2020, so VIIRS drives the recent series; the unit is burning cell-days, not hotspot counts; no independent validation yet (for example, against NOAA-20).

AI use

Parts of the code, the analysis plan, the documentation and the presentation were developed with the help of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. I ran the scripts, checked the outputs and decided what to keep.
